subject: math
title: Grade 3 Fractions and Fair Shares
seo_title: Grade 3 Fractions and Fair Shares Worksheets: Free Math Practice with Answer Key (Ontario Curriculum)
standard_text: Use drawings to represent, solve, and compare the results of fair-share problems that involve sharing up to 20 items among 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, and 10 sharers, including problems that result in whole numbers, mixed numbers, and fractional amounts
meta_desc: Free Grade 3 math worksheets on fractions and fair shares for the Ontario curriculum: name halves to tenths, share pizzas fairly, compare unit fractions and count by unit fractions. 100 questions with an answer key, great EQAO practice.
key_big: Fractions need equal parts. More sharers means smaller pieces.
key_sub: 3 pizzas shared by 4 friends: cut each pizza into fourths, and each friend gets 3/4 of a pizza. 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 3/4.
body_html:
Equal parts

A fraction is part of a whole. The whole must be cut into equal parts.

The bottom number tells how many equal parts make the whole. The top number tells how many parts you have.

Equal partsNameOne part
2halvesone half, 12
3thirdsone third, 13
4fourthsone fourth, 14
5fifthsone fifth, 15
6sixthsone sixth, 16
8eighthsone eighth, 18
10tenthsone tenth, 110

Fair shares

A fair share means everyone gets the same amount. Give out whole items first. Then cut each leftover item into as many equal pieces as there are people.

Example

12 muffins are shared by 4 friends.

12 ÷ 4 = 3. Nothing is left over.

Answer: 3 muffins each

Example

2 granola bars are shared by 3 friends.

Fewer bars than friends, so each gets less than 1. Cut each bar into thirds. Each friend gets 1 third from each bar.

Answer: 23 of a granola bar

Compare unit fractions

A unit fraction has 1 on top. More sharers means smaller pieces. So the bigger the bottom number, the smaller the fraction.

Example

Compare 13 and 15.

A whole cut into 3 parts has bigger parts than a whole cut into 5 parts.

Answer: 13 > 15

Count by unit fractions

34 means 3 fourths: 14 + 14 + 14 = 34. The parts stay fourths, so the bottom number stays 4.

Keep counting past 1 whole: 14, 24, 34, 1, 1 14. A whole number and a fraction together, like 1 14, is a mixed number.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Calling unequal parts “fourths” or “thirds”Fractions need equal parts
Thinking 18 is bigger than 14 because 8 is bigger than 4More parts means smaller parts, so 18 < 14
Writing 43 for 3 pizzas shared by 4The number of sharers goes on the bottom: 34
Leaving out the leftover: 5 sandwiches for 2 is “2 each”Cut the leftover sandwich too: 2 12 each
Adding the bottom numbers: 14 + 14 = 28The parts stay fourths: 24
Forgetting to count yourself: “Mateo and 4 friends” is 4 peopleCount everyone who shares: 5 people

faq.q: What fractions do Grade 3 students learn in Ontario?
faq.a: In the Ontario math curriculum, Grade 3 students work with halves, thirds, fourths, fifths, sixths, eighths and tenths. They use drawings to solve fair-share problems, compare unit fractions and count by unit fractions, including mixed numbers like 1 1/4.

faq.q: What is a fair-share problem in Grade 3 math?
faq.a: A fair-share problem shares items equally, like 3 pizzas shared by 4 friends. Students cut each pizza into fourths and find that each friend gets 3/4 of a pizza; the answer can be a whole number, a fraction or a mixed number.
Share the same pizza by 3 people and by 5 people. With fewer people each piece is bigger, so 1/3 is bigger than 1/5.

faq.q: Are fractions on the Grade 3 EQAO math assessment?
faq.a: The Grade 3 EQAO math assessment is based on the Ontario curriculum, and fractions are part of the Number strand, so fraction questions can appear. Practising fair shares, comparing and counting fractions with pictures helps.

items.q: 12 muffins are shared equally by 4 friends. How many muffins does each friend get?
items.e: Share 12 muffins into 4 equal groups: 12 ÷ 4 = 3. Each person gets 3 muffins.

items.q: 15 oranges are shared equally by 5 friends. How many oranges does each friend get?
items.e: Share 15 oranges into 5 equal groups: 15 ÷ 5 = 3. Each person gets 3 oranges.

items.e: First give out whole pancakes: 3 ÷ 2 = 1 each, with 1 pancake left. Cut it into 2 equal pieces. Each person gets 12 more. So each person gets 1 12 pancakes.

items.q: 5 sandwiches are shared equally by 2 friends. The shaded parts are one friend’s share. How many sandwiches does each friend get?
items.e: First give out whole sandwiches: 5 ÷ 2 = 2 each, with 1 sandwich left. Cut it into 2 equal pieces. Each person gets 12 more. So each person gets 2 12 sandwiches.

items.e: First give out whole pizzas: 4 ÷ 3 = 1 each, with 1 pizza left. Cut it into 3 equal pieces. Each person gets 13 more. So each person gets 1 13 pizzas.

items.q: 7 pizzas are shared equally by 4 friends. The shaded parts are one friend’s share. How many pizzas does each friend get?
items.e: First give out whole pizzas: 7 ÷ 4 = 1 each, with 3 pizzas left. Cut each one into 4 equal pieces. Each person gets 3 pieces, 34 more. So each person gets 1 34 pizzas.

items.q: 11 pancakes are shared equally by 4 friends. How many pancakes does each friend get?
items.e: First give out whole pancakes: 11 ÷ 4 = 2 each, with 3 pancakes left. Cut each one into 4 equal pieces. Each person gets 3 pieces, 34 more. So each person gets 2 34 pancakes.

items.q: 13 muffins are shared equally by 6 friends. How many muffins does each friend get?

items.q: 4 friends share 3 pizzas equally. Does each friend get more or less than 1 pizza?
items.e: Compare the number of pizzas with the number of people. 3 pizzas for 4 people: there are fewer pizzas than people, so each person gets less than 1 pizza (34).

items.q: 5 friends share 6 pizzas equally. Does each friend get more or less than 1 pizza?
items.e: Compare the number of pizzas with the number of people. 6 pizzas for 5 people: there are more pizzas than people, so each person gets 1 pizza and a bit more (1 15).

items.q: 4 friends share 3 granola bars equally. Each granola bar is cut into fourths. How many fourths does each friend get?
items.e: Each granola bar is cut into 4 equal pieces. Each friend gets 1 piece from each granola bar. There are 3 granola bars, so each friend gets 3 fourths, which is 34 of a granola bar.

items.q: 8 friends share 5 pies equally. Each pie is cut into eighths. How many eighths does each friend get?
items.e: Each pie is cut into 8 equal pieces. Each friend gets 1 piece from each pie. There are 5 pies, so each friend gets 5 eighths, which is 58 of a pie.

items.q: Count by thirds. What number is at the red dot?

items.q: Liam and 3 friends share 3 pizzas equally at a birthday party. How much pizza does each person get?
